title: Practice Set 9 — Built-in Functions and Expressions
description: Apply Spark's built-in function library: coalesce for null fallback, window functions for ranking and day-over-day comparison, collection functions, the performance hierarchy between built-ins and UDFs, and a mini-pipeline combining multiple function categories.

datasets.description: NordGrid meter readings with dual source columns (scada_kw, cellular_kw). 140 rows: 20 meters × 7 days. Some rows have null scada_kw (SCADA outage), some have null cellular_kw (no backup), 7 rows have both null.

columns.name: scada_kw
columns.description: Primary SCADA reading — null during outages

columns.name: cellular_kw
columns.description: Backup cellular reading — null when unavailable

characteristics.daysPerMeter: 7 consecutive days for window function tasks

tasks.title: Build NordGrid's Reading Fallback Chain

description.context: NordGrid's meters report readings through two channels: the primary SCADA feed (scada_kw) and a backup cellular connection (cellular_kw). When SCADA is down, the cellular value should be used. When both are down, the reading should default to 0.0 so downstream aggregations produce a number rather than null. The team uses coalesce() to implement this priority chain.
description.task: Read PS9_data_readings.csv (header=True, inferSchema=True). Add a column called daily_kw using coalesce() that takes the first non-null value from: scada_kw, cellular_kw, and a literal 0.0 as the final fallback. Store the result in a variable called readings. Then count how many rows ended up with daily_kw = 0.0 (meaning both sources were null) and store in both_null_count.
description.validationHint: daily_kw should never be null — coalesce guarantees a fallback to 0.0. The 7 rows where both scada_kw and cellular_kw are null should have daily_kw = 0.0.

tasks.partialCredit: 4 independent assertions. Each passed assertion earns 1/4 credit.

fields.label: Primary feed (scada_kw) and backup (cellular_kw) can both be null. How do you guarantee daily_kw is never null?
options: withColumn('daily_kw', coalesce(col('scada_kw'), col('cellular_kw'), lit(0.0))) — coalesce returns the first non-null argument; the literal 0.0 is the final guard
withColumn('daily_kw', when(col('scada_kw').isNotNull(), col('scada_kw')).otherwise(col('cellular_kw'))) — falls back to cellular when SCADA missing
na.fill(0.0, ['scada_kw']) then withColumn('daily_kw', col('scada_kw')) — pre-fill nulls and use SCADA directly
fields.correctAnswer: withColumn('daily_kw', coalesce(col('scada_kw'), col('cellular_kw'), lit(0.0))) — coalesce returns the first non-null argument; the literal 0.0 is the final guard
fields.rationale: coalesce takes any number of arguments and picks the first non-null.fill version ignores cellular_kw entirely.

tasks.title: Rank NordGrid's Meters by Consumption Within Each Region

description.context: NordGrid's operations team wants to identify the top-consuming meters within each region for capacity planning. They need a ranking where the meter with the highest average daily consumption in each region gets rank 1. The ranking must use a window function so that every meter keeps its row — unlike groupBy, no rows should be lost.
description.task: Start with the readings DataFrame. First create a daily_kw column using coalesce(scada_kw, cellular_kw, lit(0.0)). Then compute each meter's average daily_kw across all 7 days using groupBy('meter_id', 'region').agg(avg('daily_kw').alias('avg_daily_kw')). Then apply a window function with Window.partitionBy('region').orderBy(col('avg_daily_kw').desc()) to add a rank_in_region column using row_number(). Store the result in a variable called ranked.
description.validationHint: ranked should have 20 rows (one per meter). Each region's rank_in_region should start at 1. NORTH should have ranks 1–7, SOUTH 1–5, EAST 1–5, WEST 1–3.

tasks.partialCredit: 5 independent assertions. Each passed assertion earns 1/5 credit.

fields.label: Rank meters within each region by avg daily_kw, descending. Which window definition is right?
options: Window.partitionBy('region').orderBy(col('avg_daily_kw').desc()) with row_number() — partition resets the rank per region
Window.partitionBy('meter_id').orderBy('avg_daily_kw') with row_number() — partitioning by meter ID gives each meter rank 1
Window.orderBy(col('avg_daily_kw').desc()) — global ordering yields a single 1..20 ranking across all regions
fields.correctAnswer: Window.partitionBy('region').orderBy(col('avg_daily_kw').desc()) with row_number() — partition resets the rank per region
fields.rationale: partitionBy defines the rank reset boundary.Partition by region → rank resets each region.

tasks.title: Compute Day-Over-Day Consumption Change

description.context: NordGrid's anomaly detection system flags meters whose consumption changes dramatically from one day to the next. The system needs each row enriched with the previous day's reading so it can compute the day-over-day change. This requires a window function with lag() — partitioned by meter and ordered by date.
description.task: Start with the readings DataFrame. Create daily_kw using coalesce(scada_kw, cellular_kw, lit(0.0)). Define a window partitioned by meter_id and ordered by date. Use lag('daily_kw', 1) over this window to add a prev_day_kw column. Then add a daily_change column computed as daily_kw - prev_day_kw. Store the result in a variable called with_change.
description.validationHint: with_change should have 140 rows (same as input — window functions preserve row count). Each meter's first day should have null for prev_day_kw and null for daily_change (no previous day exists). The remaining 120 rows (20 meters × 6 days) should have non-null daily_change.

tasks.partialCredit: 5 independent assertions. Each passed assertion earns 1/5 credit.

fields.label: lag('daily_kw', 1) over a window partitioned by meter_id, ordered by date. Why is the FIRST row per meter null?
options: Lag references the row offset back; the first row in a partition has no predecessor, so the lag value is null and daily_change (today − null) is also null
Window functions skip the first row of each partition by design — adjusting the windowSpec to include UNBOUNDED PRECEDING fixes it
lag() requires a default value as a third argument; without it, every row returns null
fields.correctAnswer: Lag references the row offset back; the first row in a partition has no predecessor, so the lag value is null and daily_change (today − null) is also null
fields.rationale: lag at offset 1 has no value for the partition's first row — that's expected behavior.UNBOUNDED PRECEDING applies to running aggregates, not lag.

tasks.title: Predict Function Behavior: explode and greatest

description.context: Two Spark functions sound similar but work very differently. explode(array_col) is a ROW-MULTIPLYING function — it produces one OUTPUT ROW per array element, so a row with a 3-element array becomes 3 rows. The original array column is replaced by a scalar 'item' column. greatest(c1, c2, c3) is a ROW-LEVEL function — it returns the largest value AMONG the listed columns WITHIN A SINGLE ROW. Row count is unchanged. Critically, greatest is NOT the same as max(); max is an AGGREGATION that reduces a column down to one value across all rows, while greatest operates HORIZONTALLY across columns within each row.
description.task: Predict the output of each snippet and recognize the greatest vs max distinction.
description.validationHint: explode() increases the row count. greatest() compares across columns within one row (not across rows like max()).

evidence.label: Snippet A: explode
evidence.content:
df_a = spark.createDataFrame([
    ('M-001', [100.0, 200.0, 300.0]),
    ('M-002', [400.0, 500.0]),
], schema=['meter_id', 'samples'])
df_exploded = df_a.select('meter_id', explode(col('samples')).alias('sample'))

evidence.label: Snippet B: greatest
evidence.content:
df_b = spark.createDataFrame([
    ('M-001', 800.0, 1250.5, 950.0),
    ('M-002', 600.0,  870.2, 720.0),
], schema=['meter_id', 'morning_kw', 'afternoon_kw', 'evening_kw'])
df_peak = df_b.select('meter_id', greatest('morning_kw', 'afternoon_kw', 'evening_kw').alias('peak_kw'))

fields.label: Snippet A: How many rows does df_exploded have?
fields.rationale: M-001 has an array of 3 elements → 3 rows. M-002 has an array of 2 elements → 2 rows. Total: 5 rows. explode() creates one row per array element.

fields.label: Snippet A: How many columns does df_exploded have?
fields.rationale: The select keeps 'meter_id' and the exploded 'sample' column. The original 'samples' array column is not carried forward.

fields.label: Snippet B: What is the peak_kw value for M-001?
fields.rationale: greatest(800.0, 1250.5, 950.0) returns 1250.5 — the largest value across the three columns in that row.

fields.label: How does greatest() differ from max() in spark.sql.functions?
options: They are identical — both find the maximum value, with greatest being just a less-common alias for max.

greatest() compares HORIZONTALLY across multiple columns within a SINGLE row; max() aggregates VERTICALLY down ONE column across all rows. They solve different problems and produce different shapes of output.
greatest() is just faster than max() because it skips the shuffle that max() requires for aggregation.
max() works on strings while greatest() works only on numeric types; the difference is which types they support.
fields.correctAnswer: greatest() compares HORIZONTALLY across multiple columns within a SINGLE row; max() aggregates VERTICALLY down ONE column across all rows. They solve different problems and produce different shapes of output.
fields.rationale: greatest is row-level (input: N columns, output: one new column); max is aggregation (input: one column, output: one scalar per group).
fields.distractorRationale: Option A: They are not aliases; they are different operations entirely.

description.context: Spark has a strict PERFORMANCE HIERARCHY for transformations. (1) BUILT-IN FUNCTIONS (col operations, when, upper, coalesce, etc.) run at JVM speed inside Catalyst — fastest, always preferred. (2) expr() with a SQL string compiles to the same plan as built-ins — equal speed, sometimes more readable for complex CASE WHEN. (3) PANDAS UDFs use Apache Arrow to send batches of rows to Python; ~10x faster than Python UDFs and the right choice when you NEED a Python library. (4) PYTHON UDFs send one row at a time to Python — 10-100x SLOWER than built-ins. They are LAST RESORT, used only when no built-in exists AND batch processing is impossible. The decision tree: built-in if possible → expr() if clearer → Pandas UDF for Python libs → Python UDF only as a final fallback.
description.task: Pick the right approach for each transformation.
description.validationHint: The decision tree: Can a built-in do it? → Use built-in. Is SQL syntax clearer? → Use expr(). Need Python libraries? → Pandas UDF. Custom row-level logic with no built-in? → Python UDF (last resort).

evidence.title: Input sample
evidence.content: Four transformation scenarios; pick the right tier of the performance hierarchy.

fields.label: Convert daily_kw from kilowatts to megawatts (divide by 1000). Which approach?
options: Python UDF: def to_mw(kw): return kw / 1000 — UDFs are the most flexible approach for any arithmetic.
Built-in: col('daily_kw') / 1000 — basic arithmetic is what built-ins were designed for; this runs at JVM speed inside Catalyst with no serialization overhead.
expr(): expr('daily_kw / 1000') — SQL syntax is more readable for arithmetic and matches data engineer convention.
Any approach works equally — Spark optimizes UDFs, expr, and built-ins to the same plan.
fields.correctAnswer: Built-in: col('daily_kw') / 1000 — basic arithmetic is what built-ins were designed for; this runs at JVM speed inside Catalyst with no serialization overhead.
fields.rationale: Arithmetic is the canonical built-in case.col() / 1000 is the cleanest, fastest, most idiomatic option.
fields.distractorRationale:
Option A: UDFs for arithmetic are 10-100x slower with no benefit.
Option C: expr() is fine but no clearer than the built-in for division.

fields.label: Categorize meters into 6 billing tiers with complex threshold logic (CASE WHEN with 6 branches). Which approach?
options: Built-in: 6 chained when().when()...otherwise() — works but reads as a long Python expression that obscures the branching logic.
expr() with a SQL CASE WHEN — works but is non-idiomatic in PySpark code and adds a string parser to the plan.
Python UDF with if/elif chains — most readable for engineers familiar with Python.

Either built-in chain OR expr('CASE WHEN ...') is correct — both run at JVM speed inside Catalyst, so the choice is purely about which is more readable in context. Choose whichever your team finds clearer.
fields.correctAnswer: Either built-in chain OR expr('CASE WHEN ...') is correct — both run at JVM speed inside Catalyst, so the choice is purely about which is more readable in context. Choose whichever your team finds clearer.
fields.rationale: Built-in chains and expr() compile to the SAME logical plan with the SAME runtime — they are interchangeable for performance.
fields.distractorRationale: Option A: Long when chains work fine; this option's framing makes it sound wrong but it IS correct as one of two equivalent options.

fields.label: Apply a proprietary encryption algorithm from a Python library to meter_id for anonymization. No Spark built-in exists for this. Which approach?
options: Built-in: use Spark's sha2() or similar built-in hashing function as a stand-in for the proprietary algorithm.
expr() with a SQL function — write the encryption logic in SQL using string concatenation and bitwise operators.
Python UDF: wrap the proprietary library call in a row-by-row UDF since no built-in exists.
Pandas UDF: batch process the meter_id column with the Python library; ~10x faster than a row-by-row Python UDF and is the canonical answer when you need a Python library.
fields.correctAnswer: Pandas UDF: batch process the meter_id column with the Python library; ~10x faster than a row-by-row Python UDF and is the canonical answer when you need a Python library.
fields.rationale: When a Python library MUST be called, Pandas UDFs are the optimal choice — they use Arrow to ship batches to Python, amortizing the overhead.
fields.distractorRationale:
Option A: Built-in hash is a different algorithm; the requirement is the proprietary one.
Option B: expr cannot call Python libraries.

fields.label: A colleague writes a Python UDF to uppercase a string column: udf(lambda s: s.upper(), StringType()). What should the code reviewer recommend?
options: Approve — the UDF is correct, type-annotated, and readable; performance is fine for any string operation.
Replace with the built-in upper() function — identical result, 10-100x faster, no Python serialization overhead.
Replace with expr('UPPER(region)') — SQL functions are categorically faster than any other approach.
Keep the UDF but add type annotations and documentation for safety.
fields.correctAnswer: Replace with the built-in upper() function — identical result, 10-100x faster, no Python serialization overhead.
fields.rationale: upper() is a built-in for exactly this case.Wrapping it in a UDF defeats the entire performance hierarchy.
fields.distractorRationale: Option A: 10-100x slowdown matters even for trivial operations.)') works but is no better than the built-in upper(); both compile identically.

tasks.title: Build NordGrid's Enriched Analytics Pipeline

description.context: NordGrid's analytics team needs a pipeline that produces a per-meter daily report. The report must resolve which reading source to use (SCADA vs cellular), compute each meter's regional rank by average consumption, and flag meters whose daily consumption exceeds 3,000 kW as 'high_alert'. The output should be ready for the dashboard team.
description.task: Write a pipeline that: (1) reads PS9_data_readings.csv; (2) adds daily_kw using coalesce(scada_kw, cellular_kw, lit(0.0)); (3) adds daily_kw_billed using ceil(daily_kw) for billing (round up to nearest integer); (4) fills any remaining null scada_kw with 0.0 using na.fill({'scada_kw': 0.0}); (5) adds alert_flag using when(daily_kw > 3000, 'high_alert').otherwise('normal'); (6) selects final columns: meter_id, date, region, daily_kw, daily_kw_billed, alert_flag. Store in a variable called report.
description.validationHint: report should have 140 rows and 6 columns. daily_kw should never be null (coalesce). daily_kw_billed should be an integer ceiling. alert_flag should have 2 distinct values.

tasks.partialCredit: 7 independent assertions. Each passed assertion earns 1/7 credit.

conceptsCombined: Combining function categories: conditional + numeric + null-handling (Lesson 10)
synthesisNotes.rationale: This mini-pipeline combines four function categories (conditional, numeric, null-handling, column selection) into a realistic analytics output.

fields.label: Pipeline must compute daily_kw_billed = ceil(daily_kw) and alert_flag based on daily_kw > 3000. What's the order?
options: First add daily_kw via coalesce, then add daily_kw_billed using ceil(col('daily_kw')), then add alert_flag using when(col('daily_kw') > 3000, 'high_alert').otherwise('normal')
Order doesn't matter — withColumn calls are independent and Spark reorders them at execution time
Compute alert_flag first based on raw scada_kw, then coalesce — the alert should reflect the original sensor reading, not the fallback
fields.correctAnswer: First add daily_kw via coalesce, then add daily_kw_billed using ceil(col('daily_kw')), then add alert_flag using when(col('daily_kw') > 3000, 'high_alert').otherwise('normal')
fields.rationale: daily_kw_billed and alert_flag both reference daily_kw, so the coalesce step must come first.

Task 6 combines Module 4 select, Module 5 when/otherwise, and Module 9 coalesce/ceil/na.fill. These cross-module combinations follow the Synthesis/Toolkit §2.4 guidance for mini-pipeline tasks.
selfCheck.datasetNotes: PS9_data_readings.csv has 140 rows: 20 meters × 7 days with dual source columns. The dual-source design forces coalesce usage. 7 rows have both sources null, testing the full fallback chain to lit(0.0). The 7-day time series per meter enables lag/lead window functions.
